analysis.one_liner: Requires companies to safeguard personal data, tell people when it is breached, and makes hiding breaches a crime.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2015 with 13 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to four House committees, sent to two subcommittees, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required companies that hold sensitive personal information on at least 10,000 Americans — Social Security numbers, financial account numbers, health records, biometric data like fingerprints, and location history — to maintain a written data-security program and to notify anyone whose data was breached, generally within 30 days. It would have made it a federal crime, punishable by up to five years in prison, for a company to deliberately conceal a breach that causes someone at least $1,000 in economic harm, and it would have let the Justice Department, the Federal Trade Commission, and state attorneys general enforce the rules. It never got a single hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers whose personal data sits on company servers. When a company loses their Social Security number, health records, or biometric data, they would learn about it quickly, with information on what was taken and how to contact the company and credit bureaus. Stronger data security requirements would reduce the breaches that feed identity theft in the first place.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone whose personal data companies hold

how_it_helps.text: Companies holding sensitive data on 10,000 or more Americans would have to implement a comprehensive data-security program with risk assessments, access controls, encryption, and employee training [S3].

Breach victims would be notified without unreasonable delay, generally within 30 days, with details on what was compromised and toll-free numbers for the company and the major credit reporting agencies [S3].
Deliberately concealing a breach that causes someone $1,000 or more in economic harm would become a federal crime punishable by up to five years in prison [S2].
Consumers who receive a breach notice would be able to place a fraud alert on their credit files under the Fair Credit Reporting Act [S3].
The Justice Department would gain authority to seek court orders to shut down botnets that damage 100 or more computers, and to freeze property bought with proceeds of breach-related crimes [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that collect and store sensitive consumer data — retailers, online services, data brokers, and other businesses — would bear the cost of building security programs, running breach notifications, and paying civil penalties, and executives would face criminal exposure for concealment. Federal and state enforcers would bear the cost of policing the rules.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates no private right of action: a consumer whose data was breached could not sue the company under this bill; only the Justice Department, the FTC, and state attorneys general could enforce it [S3].

Civil penalties are capped at $5 million per related set of violations, with a possible additional $5 million only if the violation was willful or intentional — a modest sum for a large company, and enforcement depends entirely on government action [S3].

Companies get a 30-day window to delay notice, can postpone notification indefinitely at the request of law enforcement or intelligence agencies, and are exempt from notifying anyone if data was encrypted [S3].
Financial institutions already regulated under Gramm-Leach-Bliley and health entities regulated under HIPAA are exempt from the bill's requirements, leaving a patchwork of regimes [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have given Americans a federal floor of breach protection at a real but ordinary compliance cost to companies holding data — the kind of cost most businesses already incur to varying degrees. Its design is genuinely weaker than ideal for consumers: no right to sue, a $5 million penalty cap, broad encryption and law-enforcement exemptions, and a 30-day notice window. It sets a floor rather than a ceiling for state law, so stronger state laws survive. On balance it would help the millions of people whose data is breached each year, even if modestly.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four committees and two subcommittees and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Cicilline introduced the bill on July 8, 2015, joined by 13 cosponsors, all House Democrats [S1].
The same day it was referred to four committees — Judiciary, Energy and Commerce, Financial Services, and Budget [S5].

It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade on July 10, and to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations on July 29 [S5].
No further action of any kind was taken before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies holding Americans' personal data were better off: they avoided new security mandates, 30-day breach-notification deadlines, civil penalties, and criminal liability for concealing breaches. Consumers were left with no federal breach-notification standard, relying instead on the uneven patchwork of state laws.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 cosponsors were House Democrats, and the Republican chairmen of the committees of referral took no action to move the bill.

industries.industry: Companies holding consumer data (retailers, online services, data brokers)
industries.note: The bill would have imposed security-program requirements, 30-day breach notification, civil penalties, and criminal liability for concealing breaches on any business holding sensitive data on 10,000 or more Americans. Its interest in avoiding these costs ran against consumers' interest in learning about and preventing breaches of their data.

Companies notifying more than 5,000 breach victims would have had to alert the nationwide credit bureaus, and breach victims could have placed fraud alerts on their files. This modestly feeds breach information to the bureaus while entitling consumers to free fraud alerts.
